claim: Dense reconstruction of neuronal synaptic connectivity typically requires high-resolution 3D electron microscopy (EM) data.
source: A dense reconstruction of neuronal synaptic connectivity typically requires high-resolution 3D electron microscopy (EM) data, but EM data alone lacks functional information about neurons and synapses.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract about requirements for synaptic connectivity reconstruction.

claim: EM data alone lacks functional information about neurons and synapses.
source: A dense reconstruction of neuronal synaptic connectivity typically requires high-resolution 3D electron microscopy (EM) data, but EM data alone lacks functional information about neurons and synapses.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of EM data in the abstract.

claim: The protocol obviates the requirement of tissue permeabilization in thick tissue sections for correlative pre-embedding IHC and EM.
source: We describe a protocol that obviates the requirement of tissue permeabilization in thick tissue sections, a major impediment for correlative pre-embedding IHC and EM.
evidence: This is the main claim of the manuscript, supported by experimental data throughout the Results section.

claim: The protocol demonstrates permeabilization-free labeling of neuronal cell types in tissue sections hundreds of microns thick.
source: We demonstrate the permeabilization-free labeling of neuronal cell types, intracellular enzymes, and synaptic proteins in tissue sections hundreds of microns thick in multiple brain regions from mice while simultaneously retaining the ultrastructural integrity of the tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1-5.

claim: The protocol demonstrates permeabilization-free labeling of intracellular enzymes in tissue sections hundreds of microns thick.
source: We demonstrate the permeabilization-free labeling of neuronal cell types, intracellular enzymes, and synaptic proteins in tissue sections hundreds of microns thick in multiple brain regions from mice while simultaneously retaining the ultrastructural integrity of the tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 for ChAT labeling.

claim: The protocol demonstrates permeabilization-free labeling of synaptic proteins in tissue sections hundreds of microns thick.
source: We demonstrate the permeabilization-free labeling of neuronal cell types, intracellular enzymes, and synaptic proteins in tissue sections hundreds of microns thick in multiple brain regions from mice while simultaneously retaining the ultrastructural integrity of the tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 for Homer and synaptophysin labeling.

claim: The protocol retains ultrastructural integrity of the tissue.
source: We demonstrate the permeabilization-free labeling of neuronal cell types, intracellular enzymes, and synaptic proteins in tissue sections hundreds of microns thick in multiple brain regions from mice while simultaneously retaining the ultrastructural integrity of the tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by EM images throughout the manuscript showing intact membrane structures.

claim: Recent improvements in automating the collection of 3D electron microscopy (EM) data have dramatically increased the tissue volumes that can be acquired.
source: Recent improvements in automating the collection of 3D electron microscopy (EM) data have dramatically increased the tissue volumes that can be acquired (Briggman and Bock, 2012; Eberle et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Connectivity data derived from EM does not alone contain sufficient information about the functional properties of neurons to fully constrain biologically plausible computational models.
source: Connectivity data derived from EM, however, does not alone contain sufficient information about the functional properties of neurons to fully constrain biologically plausible computational models.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation in the field.

claim: Physiological recording from neurons in a tissue sample prior to fixation is one approach to augment EM datasets with functional information.
source: One approach to augment EM datasets with functional information is to physiologically record from neurons in a tissue sample prior to fixation (Bock et al., 2011; Briggman et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2016; Wanner and Friedrich, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work demonstrating this approach.

claim: Fluorescence immunohistochemistry (IHC) can be used to identify the constituent proteins of neuronal cell types and synapses that are key determinants of the functional properties of neurons.
source: As a complementary approach, fluorescence immunohistochemistry (IHC) can be used to identify the constituent proteins of neuronal cell types and synapses that are key determinants of the functional properties of neurons (Coons et al., 1942; Cuello et al., 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational IHC work.

claim: Post-sectioning IHC is typically employed for correlative EM because the sectioning process provides access to intracellular epitopes.
source: Post-sectioning IHC is typically employed for correlative EM because the sectioning process provides access to intracellular epitopes.
evidence: This is stated as common practice in the field.

claim: Array tomography was developed to multiplex the labeling of numerous targets in ultrathin tissue sections.
source: For example, array tomography was developed to multiplex the labeling of numerous targets in ultrathin tissue sections (Collman et al., 2015; Micheva and Smith, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to array tomography publications.

claim: Array tomography is incompatible with en bloc-based methods for collecting 3D EM data that require pre-embedding IHC.
source: However, this approach is incompatible with en bloc-based methods for collecting 3D EM data that require pre-embedding IHC, as in the case of focused ion beam scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM, Hayworth et al., 2015; Knott et al., 2008), gas cluster ion beam SEM (Hayworth et al., 2020), and serial block-face scanning electron microscopy (SBEM, Denk and Horstmann, 2004).
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation with citations to relevant EM techniques.

claim: A membrane permeabilization step with nonionic surfactants such as Triton X-100 or polysorbate 20 (Tween 20) is typically performed to enable antibody penetration into thick tissue blocks for pre-embedding IHC.
source: For pre-embedding IHC, a membrane permeabilization step with nonionic surfactants such as Triton X-100 or polysorbate 20 (Tween 20) is typically performed to enable antibody penetration into thick tissue blocks, but at the cost of degraded tissue ultrastructure (Helenius and Simons, 1975; Humbel et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as common practice with citations supporting the degradation of ultrastructure.

claim: Permeabilization with nonionic surfactants degrades tissue ultrastructure.
source: For pre-embedding IHC, a membrane permeabilization step with nonionic surfactants such as Triton X-100 or polysorbate 20 (Tween 20) is typically performed to enable antibody penetration into thick tissue blocks, but at the cost of degraded tissue ultrastructure (Helenius and Simons, 1975; Humbel et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and demonstrated in Figure 1a.

claim: The preservation of extracellular space (ECS) during chemical tissue fixation improves the penetration of antibodies into the mammalian retina using minimal permeabilization.
source: To address this limitation, we began with the observation that the preservation of extracellular space (ECS) during chemical tissue fixation improves the penetration of antibodies into the mammalian retina using minimal permeabilization (Pallotto et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Aldehyde-based fixation of the brain results in the loss of the 15–20% ECS volume fraction normally found in vivo.
source: Aldehyde-based fixation of the brain has been previously demonstrated to result in the loss of the 15–20% ECS volume fraction normally found in vivo (Van Harreveld and Malhotra, 1967).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: When detergent was omitted from the labeling protocol in perfusion-fixed sections, a gradient of fluorescently labeled somata was observed that decreased in the center of sections.
source: When detergent was omitted from the labeling protocol, we observed a gradient of fluorescently labeled somata that decreased in the center of sections, as expected, and the ultrastructural membrane integrity of the tissue remained intact (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: When detergent was omitted from the labeling protocol in perfusion-fixed sections, the ultrastructural membrane integrity of the tissue remained intact.
source: When detergent was omitted from the labeling protocol, we observed a gradient of fluorescently labeled somata that decreased in the center of sections, as expected, and the ultrastructural membrane integrity of the tissue remained intact (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: With the inclusion of Triton X-100, neuronal somata were uniformly labeled throughout the depth of perfusion-fixed sections.
source: With the inclusion of a commonly used detergent, Triton X-100, neuronal somata were uniformly labeled throughout the depth of the sections but at the cost of severely degraded membrane integrity due to lipid solubilization (Figure 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: With the inclusion of Triton X-100, membrane integrity was severely degraded due to lipid solubilization in perfusion-fixed sections.
source: With the inclusion of a commonly used detergent, Triton X-100, neuronal somata were uniformly labeled throughout the depth of the sections but at the cost of severely degraded membrane integrity due to lipid solubilization (Figure 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data shown in Figure 1a and is consistent with known effects of Triton X-100.

claim: When detergent was omitted from the protocol in ECS-preserved sections, the labeling of neuronal somata remained uniform throughout the tissue.
source: However, when detergent was omitted from the protocol, the labeling of neuronal somata in ECS-preserved sections remained uniform throughout the tissue (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The exclusion of a permeabilization step yielded intact lipid membranes in ECS-preserved sections.
source: Importantly, the exclusion of a permeabilization step yielded intact lipid membranes based on electron micrographs from the same tissue (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Nuclear exclusion of NeuN labeling was observed in non-permeabilized sections compared to permeabilized sections.
source: We noted a nuclear exclusion of the NeuN labeling in the non-permeabilized sections (Figure 1f) compared to permeabilized sections (Figure 1e), indicating nuclear membranes remained impermeant to the antibody.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1e and 1f.

claim: Nuclear membranes remained impermeant to the antibody in non-permeabilized sections.
source: We noted a nuclear exclusion of the NeuN labeling in the non-permeabilized sections (Figure 1f) compared to permeabilized sections (Figure 1e), indicating nuclear membranes remained impermeant to the antibody.
evidence: This is inferred from the nuclear exclusion pattern observed in Figure 1f.

claim: A balance between ultrastructural integrity and penetration depth was dependent on the concentrations of paraformaldehyde (PFA) and glutaraldehyde (GA) in the primary fixative solution.
source: A balance between ultrastructural integrity and penetration depth was dependent on the concentrations of paraformaldehyde (PFA) and glutaraldehyde (GA) in the primary fixative solution as expected based on the different cross-linking properties of the two aldehydes (Hopwood, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and citation to aldehyde cross-linking properties.

claim: A mixture of 4% PFA and 0.005% GA yielded a good compromise between penetration depth and EM quality.
source: A mixture of 4% PFA and 0.005% GA yielded a good compromise between penetration depth and EM quality, although small variations in the GA concentration led to similar results (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Uniform labeling was achieved when using IgG primary antibody concentrations in the range of 33–66 nM.
source: Uniform labeling was achieved when using IgG primary antibody concentrations in the range of 33–66 nM (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a.

claim: The depth of penetration increased as the fixative buffer concentration increased in ~1-mm-thick sections.
source: We observed that the depth of penetration increased as the fixative buffer concentration increased and that the highest concentration we used yielded complete penetration through 1-mm-thick sections (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The highest fixative buffer concentration used yielded complete penetration through 1-mm-thick sections.
source: We observed that the depth of penetration increased as the fixative buffer concentration increased and that the highest concentration we used yielded complete penetration through 1-mm-thick sections (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The CR+ and CB+ cell densities labeled with the permeabilization-free protocol were similar to those labeled when a permeabilization step was included.
source: The CR+ and CB+ cell densities labeled with the permeabilization-free protocol (Figure 3b) were similar to those labeled when a permeabilization step was included (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data shown in Figures 3a and 3b.

claim: The permeabilization-free protocol generally yielded nuclear exclusion of the CR and CB labeling.
source: Similar to the results with anti-NeuN, the permeabilization-free protocol generally yielded nuclear exclusion of the CR and CB labeling (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: ChAT+ axons were labeled both with and without permeabilization in tissue sections from the medial prefrontal cortex.
source: Using tissue sections from the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), we achieved labeling of ChAT+ axons both with and without permeabilization (Figure 3c, d) consistent with previous reports of the innervation patterns in the mPFC (Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3c and 3d and citation to previous work.

claim: A discontinuity of the axonal labeling was noted in the permeabilization-free sections compared to the permeabilized sections for ChAT+ axons.
source: However, we noted a discontinuity of the axonal labeling in the permeabilization-free sections (Figure 3d) compared to the permeabilized sections (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data shown in Figures 3c and 3d.

claim: The incomplete axonal labeling may be due to a narrowing of the diameter of portions of the axons presenting a hindrance to the diffusion of the antibodies.
source: We hypothesize that the incomplete axonal labeling may be due to a narrowing of the diameter of portions of the axons and therefore present a hindrance to the diffusion of the antibodies or, potentially, that myelination may limit penetration into axons.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis to explain the observed discontinuity in axonal labeling.

claim: Myelination may limit penetration into axons.
source: We hypothesize that the incomplete axonal labeling may be due to a narrowing of the diameter of portions of the axons and therefore present a hindrance to the diffusion of the antibodies or, potentially, that myelination may limit penetration into axons.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis to explain the observed discontinuity in axonal labeling.

claim: Poor labeling of PSD-95 was found without permeabilization.
source: We first attempted to label the postsynaptic density protein 95 (PSD-95), but found poor labeling without permeabilization (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments, though data is not shown.

claim: PSD-95 is within approximately 30 nm of the postsynaptic membrane.
source: Among postsynaptic proteins, super-resolution microscopy has demonstrated that PSD-95 is within approximately 30 nm of the postsynaptic membrane (Dani et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to super-resolution microscopy work.

claim: Homer is a protein found more distant, greater than 50 nm, from the postsynaptic membrane of excitatory synapses.
source: We therefore attempted to label Homer, a protein found more distant, greater than 50 nm, from the postsynaptic membrane of excitatory synapses (Dani et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to super-resolution microscopy work.

claim: The labeling pattern of Homer was similar to permeabilized sections throughout the depth of 300-μm-thick sections.
source: The labeling pattern of Homer (Figure 4b) was similar to permeabilized sections (Figure 4a) throughout the depth of 300-μm-thick sections.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data shown in Figures 4a and 4b.

claim: A larger variability in the fluorescence intensity of labeled puncta was noted in the non-permeabilized tissue compared to permeabilized tissue for Homer labeling.
source: We noted a larger variability in the fluorescence intensity of labeled puncta in the non-permeabilized tissue compared to permeabilized tissue.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the Homer labeling experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Prior to permeabilization, synaptophysin labeling density was consistent with published labeling patterns.
source: Prior to permeabilization, we observed a labeling density consistent with published labeling patterns (Figure 4c, green) (Grant et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4c and citation to previous work.

claim: Following permeabilization, synaptophysin labeling was similar at the edges of the tissue but the antibody labeling was notably absent in the center of the section.
source: Following permeabilization, the labeling pattern was similar at the edges of the tissue but the antibody labeling was notably absent in the center of the section (Figure 4c, magenta).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Treatment with Triton X-100 can lead to the extraction of synaptophysin from fixed tissue.
source: This result is consistent with the observation that treatment with Triton X-100 can lead to the extraction of synaptophysin from fixed tissue (Hannah et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Synaptophysin puncta intensities were significantly correlated between pre- and post-permeabilization labeling.
source: Puncta intensities (n = 150 puncta) were significantly correlated (linear regression t-test, p=1.5×10−8) compared to a 90° rotation of the images (p=0.86), which indicated the co-localized labeling of synaptophysin pre- and post-permeabilization.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: In the hippocampus, the CR+ subgranular band and granular cell layer positioning of CB+ neurons was observed as previously reported.
source: In the hippocampus, we observed the CR+ subgranular band and granular cell layer positioning of CB+ neurons as previously reported (Ohira et al., 2010; Figure 5a–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5a-d and citation to previous work.

claim: In the olfactory bulb, non-overlapping populations of CB+ and CR+ periglomerular cells were positively identified.
source: In the olfactory bulb, non-overlapping populations of CB+ and CR+ periglomerular cells (Panzanelli et al., 2007) were positively identified (Figure 5e–h).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5e-h and citation to previous work.

claim: Individual mitral and tufted cell neurites were readily distinguished from unlabeled neurites in the surrounding neuropil of the external plexiform layer of the olfactory bulb using HRP-DAB labeling.
source: Individual mitral and tufted cell neurites were readily distinguished from unlabeled neurites in the surrounding neuropil of the external plexiform layer of the olfactory bulb (Figure 5i).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5i.

claim: An affine transform was applied to the 2P image stack to register it to the EM slice for correlative microscopy of CB+, CR+, and TH+ interneurons.
source: An affine transform was applied to the 2P image stack to register it to the EM slice, and we were then able to identify somas in the EM slice that corresponded to the immunolabeled somata in a slice from the transformed 2P stack (Figure 6a, b, right panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by the methods described and data shown in Figure 6a-b.

claim: Somas in the EM slice corresponded to the immunolabeled somata in a slice from the transformed 2P stack.
source: An affine transform was applied to the 2P image stack to register it to the EM slice, and we were then able to identify somas in the EM slice that corresponded to the immunolabeled somata in a slice from the transformed 2P stack (Figure 6a, b, right panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6a-b.

claim: TH+ axons were identified within the EM volume that matched trajectories of fluorescent axons.
source: We then locally searched regions of the EM dataset to identify the matching trajectories of fluorescent axons to those in the EM volume (Figure 6d, e) and identified TH+ axons within the EM volume (Figure 6f, g).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6d-g.

claim: The traced axons spanned a depth of 57–70 μm deep within the tissue section.
source: The traced axons spanned a depth of 57–70 μm deep within the tissue section.
evidence: This is stated as a measurement from the correlative EM experiment.

claim: The method depends on the preservation of ECS during tissue fixation.
source: The method depends on the preservation of ECS during tissue fixation (Figures 1 and 2), and we suggest that the simplest explanation for the improved labeling is that the diffusion spaces that are preserved allow antibodies to diffuse deep into tissue and travel to close proximity of their antigens.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The diffusion spaces that are preserved allow antibodies to diffuse deep into tissue and travel to close proximity of their antigens.
source: The method depends on the preservation of ECS during tissue fixation (Figures 1 and 2), and we suggest that the simplest explanation for the improved labeling is that the diffusion spaces that are preserved allow antibodies to diffuse deep into tissue and travel to close proximity of their antigens.
evidence: This is stated as the authors' interpretation of the mechanism.

claim: Rather than translocating across multiple plasma membranes in densely packed neuropil, an antibody in ECS-preserved tissue could, in principle, only need to cross one membrane to reach an epitope.
source: That is, rather than translocating across multiple plasma membranes in densely packed neuropil, an antibody in ECS-preserved tissue could, in principle, only need to cross one membrane to reach an epitope.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical explanation for the improved antibody penetration.

claim: Aldehyde fixation alone has been described to semi-permeabilize membranes due to their denaturizing effects on proteins.
source: First, aldehyde fixation alone has been described to semi-permeabilize membranes due to their denaturizing effects on proteins (Hopwood, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The hydrodynamic radius of an IgG antibody is approximately 5 nm.
source: Second, the hydrodynamic radius of an IgG antibody is approximately 5 nm (Armstrong et al., 2004; Jøssang et al., 1988), meaning a small pore in a membrane of similar size is required to provide access to intracellular epitopes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A small pore in a membrane of similar size to the hydrodynamic radius of an IgG antibody is required to provide access to intracellular epitopes.
source: Second, the hydrodynamic radius of an IgG antibody is approximately 5 nm (Armstrong et al., 2004; Jøssang et al., 1988), meaning a small pore in a membrane of similar size is required to provide access to intracellular epitopes.
evidence: This is inferred from the size of IgG antibodies.

claim: A current limitation of the protocol is the inability to label antigens that are closely associated with lipid membranes such as the postsynaptic protein PSD-95.
source: A current limitation of the protocol is our inability to label antigens that are closely associated with lipid membranes such as the postsynaptic protein PSD-95.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation based on experimental observations.

claim: The ability to label the Homer protein, which is more distant from the postsynaptic membrane than PSD-95, suggests a steric hindrance for antibody binding when a protein is in close proximity to the plasma membrane.
source: The postsynaptic terminal is densely packed with protein, and our ability to label the Homer protein, which is more distant from the postsynaptic membrane than PSD-95 (Dani et al., 2010), suggests a steric hindrance for antibody binding when a protein is in close proximity to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential labeling success of Homer vs PSD-95.

claim: Some degree of permeabilization may be a requirement for proteins that are located in close spatial proximity to the plasma membrane.
source: Therefore, some degree of permeabilization may be a requirement for proteins that are located in close spatial proximity to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the PSD-95 labeling results.

claim: The use of nanobodies may improve labeling in combination with the protocol if the size of IgG antibodies is limiting the binding to postsynaptic targets.
source: Alternatively, if the size of IgG antibodies is limiting the binding to postsynaptic targets, the use of physically smaller antibodies, such as nanobodies (Hamers-Casterman et al., 1993), may improve labeling in combination with our protocol.
evidence: This is stated as a potential future direction with citation to nanobody work.

claim: Nanobodies have been shown to label targets up to 100 μm, but not deeper, from one surface of a tissue section.
source: Nanobodies have recently been shown to label targets up to 100 μm, but not deeper, from one surface of a tissue section (Fang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: An important future goal is to achieve ECS preservation by perfusion of a whole brain and uniform permeabilization-free antibody labeling throughout large tissue volumes.
source: While we focused on section thicknesses up to 1 mm, an important future goal is to achieve ECS preservation by perfusion of a whole brain (Cragg, 1980) and uniform permeabilization-free antibody labeling throughout large tissue volumes.
evidence: This is stated as a future goal with citation to previous work on ECS preservation.

claim: It is important to first confirm that ECS preservation during acute section immersion fixation was successful, ideally by inspection of EM images.
source: To replicate the protocol, we emphasize that it is important to first confirm that ECS preservation during acute section immersion fixation was successful, ideally by inspection of EM images.
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation for protocol replication.

claim: The degree of ECS preservation varies by brain region.
source: The degree of ECS preservation varies by brain region as previously reported (Pallotto et al., 2015) and needs to be calibrated for specific brain regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Refixing the tissue with 2% PFA before serially incubating in fructose solutions retains ultrastructural quality.
source: We confirmed that refixing the tissue with 2% PFA before serially incubating in fructose solutions retains ultrastructural quality (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The use of SeeDB clearing allowed obtaining two-photon (2P) excited fluorescence signals throughout the depth of 300 μm fixed tissue sections.
source: The use of SeeDB clearing allowed us to obtain two-photon (2P) excited fluorescence signals throughout the depth of 300 μm fixed tissue sections (Denk et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated as a result of using the SeeDB clearing method with citation.

claim: C57BL/6J male mice (age p30–p45) were used for all experiments except for specific transgenic lines.
source: C57BL/6J male mice (age p30–p45) were used for all experiments except for the use of Cdhr1-cre mice (Gensat stock # 030952-UCD; Nagai et al., 2005), age p50, to label mitral and tufted cells (Figure 5) and Olfr160-IRES-ChR2-YFP mice (JAX stock # 021206; Smear et al., 2013), age p42, to label interneurons in the mouse olfactory bulb (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: All animal procedures were conducted in accordance with US National Institutes of Health guidelines, as approved by the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke Animal Care and Use Committee (ASP 1340).
source: All animal procedures were conducted in accordance with US National Institutes of Health guidelines, as approved by the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke Animal Care and Use Committee (ASP 1340).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.
